name: Basic Biology of the Cardiovascular System

clinicalPearls: The heart arises from crescent-shaped fields of lateral splanchnic mesoderm; a primary (first) heart field forms the linear heart tube while a second heart field, marked by Islet-1 expression, later adds myocardium to the inflow/outflow poles and contributes much of the right ventricle and outflow tract.

Neural crest cells are required for aortic arch remodeling and truncus arteriosus septation; because these cells are sensitive to vitamin A and folic acid, maternal deficiency of these vitamins is associated with congenital defects of aortic arch remodeling.

Coronary arteries depend on epicardial cells derived from the proepicardial organ (a septum transversum derivative that also forms the fibrous diaphragm and contributes to the liver), which supply coronary smooth muscle and help pattern the vessels.

The cardiac conduction system differentiates from cardiomyocyte precursors into slow-conducting proximal components (SA and AV nodes) and fast-conducting distal components (His bundle, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers); developmental defects can produce congenital heart block or pre-excitation (Wolff-Parkinson-White).
Decremental conduction across the AV node delays atrial-to-ventricular impulse transmission to allow sequential contraction and protects the ventricle by limiting transmission of rapid atrial rates.

The endothelium is a selectively permeable barrier and a major homeostatic organ: under physiologic conditions it favors vasodilation, an antithrombotic/profibrinolytic state, anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties; endothelial dysfunction reverses each of these (vasoconstriction, prothrombotic, proinflammatory, prooxidant, impaired barrier).

Endothelium-derived vasodilators include nitric oxide (NO), prostacyclin, endothelium-derived hyperpolarizing factor, and hydrogen peroxide; flow-mediated dilatation (brachial artery cuff occlusion/release with ultrasound) is used to assess endothelial vasodilator function in humans.

Excess reactive oxygen species (e.g., superoxide generated under high angiotensin II exposure) inactivate NO, and inflammatory stimuli/endotoxin/angiotensin II drive endothelial production of PAI-1 and tissue factor, shifting balance toward thrombosis (contributing to DIC in sepsis and to hyperglycemia-related prothrombotic states).

Vascular smooth-muscle contraction is governed by cytosolic calcium and the balance of myosin light chain kinase (calcium/calmodulin-activated) versus myosin light chain phosphatase; voltage-dependent L-type calcium channels and IP3-triggered sarcoplasmic reticulum release raise intracellular calcium.

Cardiac contraction follows the sliding-filament model: an L-type calcium current during the action potential plateau triggers calcium-induced calcium release from the SR via the ryanodine receptor RyR2; calcium binds troponin C, relieving troponin-tropomyosin inhibition so actin and myosin cross-bridge cycling (ATP-dependent) can occur.

Relaxation depends on lowering cytosolic calcium by SR reuptake via SERCA2A (regulated by phospholamban) and sarcolemmal Na+/Ca2+ exchange; PKA phosphorylation of phospholamban speeds reuptake and produces the lusitropic (enhanced relaxation) effect.

Cytoplasmic calcium is the principal determinant of inotropic state: positive inotropes such as digitalis glycosides and beta-adrenergic agonists act by raising cytosolic calcium (beta agonists via Gs-adenylyl cyclase-cyclic AMP-PKA phosphorylation of sarcolemmal calcium channels).

Ventricular stroke volume is set by three factors: preload (muscle length at contraction onset), afterload (tension developed during contraction), and contractility; contractile force is optimal near a sarcomere length of about 2.2 micrometers, the structural basis of the Frank-Starling relationship.
harrison.pathophysiology: The cardiovascular system develops from cardiac progenitors in lateral splanchnic mesoderm that fuse into a linear heart tube of endocardium and spontaneously beating cardiomyocytes, then undergo asymmetric looping and chamber specification with continued addition of second-heart-field cells (Islet-1 positive). Septation separates the cardiac chambers and divides the truncus arteriosus into aorta and pulmonary artery; endocardial cushions, rich in hyaluronic-acid 'cardiac jelly', undergo epithelial-mesenchymal transformation to form valves. Neural crest cells direct aortic arch remodeling and supply smooth muscle to the great vessels, while proepicardial cells form coronary vasculature. Blood vessels share a trilaminar architecture (intimal endothelium, smooth-muscle media, fibroblast-rich adventitia), with capillaries reduced to an endothelial tube and pericytes and large vessels nourished by vasa vasorum. The endothelium maintains vascular homeostasis through balanced production of vasodilators (NO, prostacyclin) and vasoconstrictors (endothelin), regulation of leukocyte adhesion, and modulation of coagulation; loss of these functions underlies atherosclerosis, hypertension, capillary-leak states, and immune-mediated vascular injury. Vascular smooth-muscle tone is set by intracellular calcium and myosin light chain phosphorylation, integrated through sympathetic, parasympathetic, and nonadrenergic/noncholinergic (nitrergic, peptidergic) autonomic signaling. In the myocardium, the sarcomere is the contractile unit; excitation-contraction coupling links the action potential and T-tubular calcium entry to RyR2-mediated SR calcium release, troponin C activation, and actin-myosin cross-bridge cycling, with relaxation driven by SERCA2A reuptake and Na+/Ca2+ exchange. Cardiac output reflects the interplay of preload, afterload, and contractility (Frank-Starling mechanism).
additionalInvestigations: Flow-mediated dilatation of the brachial artery by ultrasound (cuff occlusion/release) to assess endothelial vasodilator function in vivo
redFlags: Inherited or acquired disturbances of SR calcium handling (RyR2/regulatory protein abnormalities) can impair contraction and predispose to heart failure or ventricular arrhythmias.

Mutations in sarcomeric and cytoskeletal proteins (including titin, dystrophin/dystroglycan complex) cause Mendelian cardiomyopathies and sensitize the heart to toxic insults such as alcohol or chemotherapy and to inflammatory or peripartum cardiomyopathy.
Developmental conduction-system defects may present as congenital heart block or pre-excitation (Wolff-Parkinson-White).
harrison.prognosis: As a foundational chapter, prognosis is framed at the level of mechanism: increased arterial stiffness with aging or disease raises left ventricular afterload and portends a poor outcome, and sustained high-flow states (e.g., left-to-right shunts) drive pulmonary smooth-muscle proliferation and pulmonary hypertension. Outcomes in specific cardiovascular diseases are detailed in their respective chapters.
pitfalls: Treating these molecular and developmental concepts as purely theoretical: shared embryonic origins of cardiovascular cell types explain syndromic associations between congenital heart disease and extracardiac anomalies.

Overlooking that true regeneration of a complete three-layered blood vessel does not normally occur in adult mammals, so adult arteriogenesis/angiogenesis reflects growth and collateral expansion rather than new full-thickness vessel formation.

Assuming adult vascular smooth-muscle cells are quiescent; they proliferate and migrate after injury or inflammatory activation, contributing to atherosclerotic stenosis, hypertensive arteriolar remodeling, and restenosis.
management: Modification of cardiovascular risk factors, with smoking cessation, statin lipid-lowering, blood-pressure control and glycaemic control, to shift dysfunctional endothelium back toward its vasodilatory, antithrombotic state
Blood-pressure control to limit progressive arterial stiffening and reduce left ventricular afterload
Timely closure of significant left-to-right shunts before irreversible pulmonary vascular remodelling and Eisenmenger physiology develop
Permanent pacing for congenital heart block arising from conduction-system developmental defects
Catheter ablation of accessory pathways and avoidance of AV-nodal blocking drugs in Wolff-Parkinson-White pre-excitation
Antenatal optimisation of folic acid and vitamin A status to support neural-crest-dependent outflow tract and aortic arch development
Multidisciplinary cardiology and congenital heart disease follow-up
